cards.term: Always a bridesmaid, never a bride
cards.hint: always supporting, never getting the spotlight
cards.meaning: To play a supportive role while consistently missing out on the main reward or recognition.
cards.nuance: It often expresses mild frustration, but it can also be humorous or self-aware. Because it refers to wedding roles, modern speakers may use it to describe any situation where someone reliably does the supporting work.
cards.literal: A woman is invited to attend a wedding as a bridesmaid but is never chosen to be the bride.

uses.sentence: I organize every launch event, but I’m always a bridesmaid, never a bride when the team gets recognized.
uses.highlight: always a bridesmaid, never a bride
uses.tip: It adds humor, but consider naming the recognition you want directly.

uses.where: Wedding reception · reflecting on a familiar role
uses.sentence: I’m always a bridesmaid, never a bride, so I’ve become the expert at keeping celebrations on schedule.
uses.highlight: always a bridesmaid, never a bride
uses.tip: Use it playfully when you are comfortable being the dependable guest.

uses.where: Lighthearted team update · describing a supporting role
uses.sentence: I may be always a bridesmaid, never a bride, but someone has to coordinate every detail.
uses.highlight: always a bridesmaid, never a bride
uses.tip: Keep it light; this can sound resentful if the context is already serious.

origin.summary: The saying grew from humorous rhymes and songs about bridesmaids, who traditionally support the bride rather than take the central role. Its exact first appearance is difficult to pin down, so its broader origin is best treated as likely.

timeline.text: Short comic verses about bridesmaids circulate, often contrasting their supporting role with the bride’s central role.
Variations of “always the bridesmaid, never the bride” become familiar in popular songs and conversation.
The expression is used beyond weddings for anyone who feels consistently helpful but overlooked.

similar: always the bridesmaid, never the bride
cards.pitfall: The phrase can sound self-pitying or imply that you never want a leading role, so avoid it when discussing someone else’s frustration.

cards.term: always the bridesmaid, never the bride
cards.hint: always supporting, never getting the spotlight
cards.meaning: To always play a supporting role while never being the main person or receiving the main benefit.
cards.nuance: It can sound playful and self-aware, but sometimes carries frustration about being overlooked. The wording reflects traditional wedding roles, so it may feel dated or overly gendered in some contexts.
cards.literal: A bridesmaid helps the bride at a wedding but is not the bride herself.

uses.sentence: I organized the launch, but I’m always the bridesmaid, never the bride when awards are announced.
uses.highlight: always the bridesmaid, never the bride
uses.tip: Use it lightly when you want recognition without sounding openly resentful.

uses.sentence: I end up handling every detail, always the bridesmaid, never the bride of the evening.
uses.highlight: always the bridesmaid, never the bride
uses.tip: It works well among friends when you’re jokingly noting that someone else takes the spotlight.

uses.sentence: You were always the bridesmaid, never the bride, yet your support kept the whole team moving.
uses.highlight: always the bridesmaid, never the bride
uses.tip: It can add a playful metaphor, but a direct compliment may sound more sincere.

origin.summary: Probably grew from the familiar contrast between a bridesmaid’s supporting role and the bride’s central role. The wording later became a popular way to describe people who regularly help others but receive less attention.

timeline.text: Bridesmaids were widely understood as attendants whose job was to support the bride.
The contrasting pair became a familiar metaphor for supporting other people without being the center of attention.
It remains common in personal, workplace and humorous expressions.

cards.pitfall: The phrase can sound self-deprecating or resentful, and its wedding imagery may feel traditional or outdated in some settings.

cards.term: ashes to ashes, dust to dust
cards.hint: a solemn reminder of death and return to the earth
cards.meaning: A traditional funeral phrase expressing the idea that the dead return to the earth and the cycle of life continues.
cards.nuance: It is used at funerals, in burial services and in serious reflections on mortality. Outside a religious setting, it may sound poetic, sombre or old-fashioned.
cards.literal: A person’s remains go from the burning of the body to dust, and the body returns to the ground from which it came.

uses.sentence: At her memorial, the family reflected on her kindness with the words, “ashes to ashes, dust to dust.”
uses.highlight: ashes to ashes, dust to dust
uses.tip: Keep the tone respectful and avoid using it as a casual metaphor at work.

uses.sentence: The minister spoke gently, and the congregation repeated together, “ashes to ashes, dust to dust.”
uses.highlight: ashes to ashes, dust to dust
uses.tip: Use it when the ritual or the family has established that it fits.

uses.sentence: Her warmth will stay with everyone who knew her, even as we accept the hard truth of ashes to ashes, dust to dust.
uses.highlight: ashes to ashes, dust to dust
uses.tip: Pair it with genuine sympathy rather than making it the main message.

origin.summary: The phrase comes from Christian burial language and combines the traditional ideas of the body becoming ashes and returning as dust. Its familiar wording is preserved in the English funeral service, while the idea that human beings return to dust also echoes Genesis 3:19.

timeline.text: Funeral traditions developed around cremation, burial and the body’s return to dust.
The Book of Common Prayer included the committal words “earth to earth, ashes to ashes, dust to dust.”
The shorter phrase remains common in funerals, memorials and sombre reflections on death.

cards.pitfall: The phrase carries strong associations with death and burial, so it can sound insensitive or melodramatic if used jokingly or casually.

cards.term: be careful what you wish for
cards.hint: getting what you wanted may not be good
cards.meaning: A warning that getting something you want could lead to unexpected problems or an unwanted result.
cards.nuance: It can be playful, stern or sarcastic, depending on the situation. Use it when the possible downside of a wish or request is significant.
cards.literal: Be cautious about asking for something, because what arrives may cause trouble.

uses.where: Team discussion · taking on extra work
uses.sentence: You’re asking to lead the entire project? Be careful what you wish for.
uses.highlight: Be careful what you wish for
uses.tip: This adds light warning without directly saying the request is a bad idea.

uses.where: Conversation with a friend · weekend plans
uses.sentence: She asked for a quiet holiday, so I told her to be careful what she wished for.
uses.highlight: be careful what she wished for
uses.tip: Use this when the outcome may be enjoyable but more demanding than expected.

uses.where: Message to a friend · planning a celebration
uses.sentence: You wanted the loudest party possible, so be careful what you wish for.
uses.highlight: be careful what you wish for
uses.tip: Keep the tone friendly unless you are clearly warning someone about a serious risk.

origin.summary: The phrase comes from an old idea that spoken wishes can bring unwanted consequences. It entered everyday English through stories and sayings about dangerous wishes, with its modern form well established by the 20th century.

timeline.text: Stories and proverbs warned that some wishes could lead to danger or misfortune.
The wording “be careful what you wish for” became established in English-language warnings.
It is widely used in conversation, sometimes humorously and sometimes seriously.

similar: you may get what you asked for
be careful what you ask for
the grass is greener on the other side
cards.pitfall: The phrase is usually a warning after someone expresses a wish; it does not necessarily mean the wish will literally come true.

cards.meaning: To feel grateful for small but unexpected signs of kindness, luck, or relief during a difficult situation.
cards.nuance: It often sounds mildly humorous, relieved, or a little weary. It works when a small convenience or good outcome feels especially welcome, though it can sound old-fashioned in very formal writing.
cards.literal: Being grateful for small acts of kindness or modest pieces of good fortune.

uses.sentence: When the vendor backup held and nobody had to rebuild the report, I was thankful for small mercies.
uses.tip: Use it when genuine relief follows a stressful period.

uses.sentence: The rain stopped just as we reached the café, so I was thankful for small mercies.
uses.tip: It adds a self-aware, slightly humorous note to casual conversation.

uses.sentence: The appointment was sooner than expected, and I was thankful for small mercies.
uses.tip: Use it to express understated relief, not to minimise a serious problem.

origin.summary: The expression developed from the older idea of a “small mercy,” meaning a minor kindness or act of leniency. Its modern form combines that older wording with a more explicit attitude of gratitude.

timeline.text: A “small mercy” meant a modest act of kindness, forgiveness, or relief.
English writers used “small mercies” for welcome reliefs during difficult circumstances.
The expression developed into its familiar grateful, often mildly ironic, modern form.

similar: be grateful for what you have
cards.pitfall: In serious hardship, this can sound flippant unless the surrounding context makes the relief genuinely minor.

cards.hint: too focused on the past to see the present clearly
cards.meaning: So attached to memories of the past that you overlook problems or limitations in the present.
cards.nuance: Often used about a person, place or relationship that once seemed better. It can be affectionate and nostalgic, or critical when the past is being used to avoid change.
cards.literal: Unable to see clearly because the past is dazzling, vivid or emotionally overpowering.

uses.sentence: We were blinded by nostalgia for the old process, even though the new one saved everyone hours.
uses.tip: Use it when examining why people prefer an outdated process.

uses.sentence: She was blinded by nostalgia and kept calling me by the nickname we used as teenagers.
uses.tip: It usually adds a thoughtful or slightly teasing tone.

uses.where: Travel article · contrasting old and new neighbourhoods
uses.sentence: The author is not entirely blinded by nostalgia, and she acknowledges what the redevelopment has displaced.
uses.tip: It works well for balancing affection for the past with an honest look at change.

origin.summary: Likely developed from older expressions such as “blinded by love,” applying the idea of emotional dazzlingness to nostalgia.

timeline.text: Writers used “blinded by” for being unable to judge clearly because of a powerful emotion.
The form “blinded by nostalgia” emerged for idealising the past while overlooking present realities.
It appears in reflective, literary and cultural criticism.

cards.pitfall: The phrase suggests distorted judgement, so it may sound too harsh when you are simply remembering something fondly.

cards.hint: suddenly feel panic or lose confidence
cards.register: Common at work and in everyday conversation
cards.meaning: To suddenly panic, feel intensely frightened, or lose all confidence.
cards.nuance: It suggests a sharp emotional collapse rather than ordinary worry. It can describe a moment of panic or a situation that makes someone feel as though everything has become overwhelming.
cards.literal: The supporting surface suddenly falls away, leaving nothing solid beneath you.

uses.where: Team stand-up · a major client changes direction
uses.sentence: When the client postponed the launch, I thought the bottom drops out of my stomach.
uses.tip: Use it for a sudden emotional reaction, not routine stress.

uses.where: At a party · your friends leave unexpectedly
uses.sentence: Everyone went home early, and it felt like the bottom drops out of the evening.
uses.tip: This version can describe a situation collapsing rather than your emotions.

uses.sentence: For a moment, I felt like the bottom drops out of my world when I heard the news.
uses.tip: Usually use the past tense, “the bottom dropped out,” in finished writing.

origin.summary: The expression probably grew from a literal image of something losing its support. Writers later applied it to sudden fear, emotional shock, and situations that seemed to collapse.

timeline.text: The literal image was of a bottom or foundation suddenly giving way.
The expression developed figurative meanings involving fear, shock, and sudden collapse.
It remains common for describing panic or a dramatic emotional change.

similar: feel like the world is ending
cards.pitfall: The common form is “the bottom drops out of my stomach.” Avoid “the bottom drops out” when you mean only that something is gradually becoming less stable.

cards.term: butter wouldn't melt in someone's mouth
cards.hint: looks too innocent to be guilty
cards.meaning: Someone appears so gentle, harmless or well behaved that they could hardly be suspected of wrongdoing.
cards.nuance: It often implies that a person is pretending to be innocent while hiding cunning or dishonest behaviour. It can also be used more lightly to describe someone who seems unusually polite.
cards.literal: The exaggerated image of butter staying firm in a warm mouth suggests that the person is too innocent or harmless to be capable of wrongdoing.

uses.sentence: He appears helpful, but some staff think butter wouldn't melt in someone's mouth.
uses.highlight: butter wouldn't melt in someone's mouth
uses.tip: Use it when you strongly suspect someone is managing how they appear.

uses.sentence: My friend was charming all evening; you might think butter wouldn't melt in someone's mouth.
uses.highlight: butter wouldn't melt in someone's mouth
uses.tip: The phrase can sound playful until it suggests deliberate deception.

uses.where: Opinion column · questioning a public figure
uses.sentence: Calling the minister harmless was like saying butter wouldn't melt in someone's mouth.
uses.highlight: butter wouldn't melt in someone's mouth
uses.tip: It conveys scepticism, so place it where the surrounding context supports that doubt.

origin.summary: The expression probably developed from exaggerated descriptions of innocence and harmlessness. Its exact earliest wording is uncertain, but the figurative sense was established by the 19th century.

timeline.text: People used vivid comparisons to describe someone as exceptionally mild, innocent or harmless.
Figurative expressions began appearing in print that compared an innocent-looking person's mouth with melting butter.
The wording settled into the familiar expression used today.

cards.pitfall: The phrase describes an appearance and often challenges that appearance; it does not provide proof that someone is dishonest.

cards.meaning: Do not worry about a problem or situation; it is not serious enough to concern you.
cards.nuance: Friendly, reassuring and informal, especially useful when someone is stressed about something minor. It can sound dismissive if the problem is genuinely serious.
cards.literal: Do not become tense or anxious about it.

uses.where: Colleague asks about a small delay
uses.sentence: The report is due tomorrow, not today—don't sweat it.
uses.tip: Use it for a manageable problem, not to brush aside a major concern.

uses.where: Friend is nervous about a dinner plan
uses.sentence: We can order takeaway if we miss the reservation; don't sweat it.
uses.tip: It sounds warm and supportive when someone needs a little reassurance.

uses.where: Text message after a minor mix-up
uses.sentence: I found the missing file—don't sweat it.
uses.tip: It works in a casual message when you want to sound relaxed and kind.

origin.summary: The wording likely comes from the older idea of sweating as a sign of anxiety or worry. The exact first recorded use is uncertain, but the phrase became established in informal American English.

timeline.text: Sweating was used figuratively for feeling worried or nervous.
The phrase settled into informal speech as a reassuring response to minor worries.
It remains common in casual American English, especially in speech and texts.

cards.pitfall: Avoid saying “don't sweat it” when the person faces a serious problem, since it can make their concern feel invalid.

cards.hint: reassurance that things will be fine
cards.meaning: You do not need to be concerned, because the situation is likely to be handled or turn out well.
cards.nuance: It is warm and reassuring, but it can sound vague if the person has asked for advice or a real solution.

uses.sentence: Don't worry, we've got enough time to finish the report properly.
uses.tip: Follow it with a specific reassurance so it does not sound like empty reassurance.

uses.where: Friend is nervous about an event
uses.sentence: Don't worry, everyone will be nervous at first, and it'll be fine once you arrive.
uses.tip: This is friendly and casual; offer a practical detail if the person seems genuinely uneasy.

uses.where: Reassuring a client about a small delay
uses.sentence: Don't worry—we're on track to deliver the files by Friday as planned.
uses.tip: Use it in a personal note; formal business writing often prefers “There’s no need to worry.”

origin.summary: This is a modern everyday expression built from the older words “do not” and “worry.” Its reassuring use became common as spoken and informal written language expanded.

timeline.text: The words “worry” and “do not” were used together to advise someone not to be concerned.
The shortened form “don't worry” became common in casual speech and informal writing.
It is used widely as a reassuring phrase, especially in everyday conversation and personal messages.

cards.pitfall: When someone explains a serious problem, don't worry may sound dismissive; acknowledge the issue before offering reassurance.

cards.meaning: You feel embarrassed because you think people are talking about you or noticing something you would rather keep private.
cards.nuance: It describes an instant, uncomfortable reaction to imagined attention. It can be playful or sincere, but it often suggests that the speaker feels exposed rather than simply pleased to be noticed.
cards.literal: The physical feeling of your ears becoming hot, usually understood as a sign of embarrassment or shame.

uses.where: Team chat · accidentally missing a message
uses.sentence: I sent the client the wrong file, and now my ears are burning.
uses.tip: Use it to acknowledge a small embarrassment with light self-deprecation.

uses.where: Leaving a gathering · realizing a mistake
uses.sentence: Only when I got home did I remember that I had replied to the wrong person, so my ears are burning.
uses.tip: It adds humor when you admit an awkward mistake after the moment has passed.

uses.where: Informal message · reacting to unexpected praise
uses.sentence: My manager mentioned my presentation in the team meeting, and now my ears are burning.
uses.tip: Keep it conversational; it usually works better in a message among people who know you well.

origin.summary: The expression likely comes from the physical sensation of hot or burning ears during embarrassment. The figurative use developed in English before the modern era and remains common in everyday speech.

timeline.text: People noticed that embarrassment or shame could make the ears feel hot.
Writers used descriptions of burning ears to express embarrassment or the feeling of being exposed.
The expression is widely understood as a quick way to describe sudden embarrassment.

cards.pitfall: It usually means you feel embarrassed, not that you have literally harmed your ears; it is also not proof that people are talking about you.

cards.hint: as a reminder of earlier days
cards.meaning: Doing something because it brings back memories of an earlier time or relationship.
cards.nuance: It often carries warm, nostalgic feelings and is especially common among family members, old friends or former colleagues.
cards.literal: Doing something for the sake of times that have passed.

uses.where: Team gathering · revisiting an old project
uses.sentence: We kept the original logo for old time's sake, but everyone agrees we should update it now.
uses.tip: Use it when nostalgia is part of the reason for keeping or repeating something.

uses.sentence: We played our usual songs for old time's sake and ended up talking until midnight.
uses.tip: It sounds affectionate and slightly sentimental among people who share a past.

uses.sentence: I copied you on this announcement for old time's sake, since we worked together when it was first planned.
uses.tip: It gives a personal touch when marking a shared memory without dwelling on it.

origin.summary: The phrase likely grew from the older expression “old times,” meaning earlier days. Its sentimental sense became established in the 19th century and later became common in personal and social speech.

timeline.text: “Old times” referred broadly to the past, especially times remembered with affection.
The expression developed into a familiar way of justifying something nostalgic or traditional.
It is used to explain affectionate gestures toward earlier experiences or shared memories.

cards.pitfall: The more traditional wording is “for old times' sake”; “for old time's sake” is a less usual variant.

cards.hint: jealous of what someone else has
cards.meaning: Feeling jealous because someone else has something you want.
cards.nuance: It emphasizes a strong, visible sense of jealousy or desire for what another person has. It can sound playful among friends but slightly dramatic in formal settings.
cards.literal: Looking pale or ill with a greenish color caused by envy.

uses.where: Promotion announcement · reacting to a colleague
uses.sentence: She was green with envy when she heard that her teammate had won the award.
uses.tip: Use it about feelings, not as a direct criticism of the colleague.

uses.sentence: I was green with envy when they showed photos of their sunlit weekend away.
uses.tip: It works well in a lighthearted conversation when admitting jealousy.

uses.sentence: I know it sounds silly, but I was absolutely green with envy of her new kitchen.
uses.tip: Pair it with “of” plus the person or thing you envy.

origin.summary: The expression developed from the idea that extreme jealousy could make someone look pale or sickly. Its exact first use is uncertain, but similar wording appears in older English.

timeline.text: Older expressions associated jealousy with changes in a person's complexion.
Writers used variations describing someone as green, pale or sick with envy.
The fixed phrase remains common in everyday conversation.

cards.pitfall: Usually describe the envious person, not the person being envied: “I was green with envy of her success.”

cards.hint: a good wish before something difficult
cards.meaning: A friendly wish for someone to have a successful outcome.
cards.nuance: It is especially used before a performance, competition, interview or other challenging event. In British, Irish and Australian speech, it can sound warmer and more personal than “good luck.”

uses.sentence: Here’s luck with your presentation this afternoon.
uses.tip: Use it when the person is about to face a demanding task.

uses.where: Supporting a friend before a talent show
uses.sentence: Here’s luck—you’re going to be brilliant up there.
uses.tip: A dash lets you add encouragement without interrupting the well-wish.

uses.where: Message before a friend’s job interview
uses.sentence: Here’s luck with the interview—I’m sure you’ll do well.
uses.tip: It sounds friendly but slightly more personal than a formal “good luck.”

origin.summary: A shortened form of “here’s luck to you,” used as a cheerful wish of success. The expression is especially associated with British and Irish speech.

timeline.text: The older wish “luck to you” expresses the hope that an outcome will be favourable.
The shortened form “here’s luck” appears in English speech and writing.
It remains a warm, informal way to wish someone success before a difficult event.

cards.pitfall: It is most natural before an event; after an unsuccessful outcome, people usually say “better luck next time.”

cards.meaning: To say that you understand someone’s feelings, situation or point of view.
cards.nuance: It is warm, informal and supportive, though it can also show casual agreement. It works best when you acknowledge the person’s experience or explain what you understand.

uses.where: Team check-in · a colleague sounds overwhelmed
uses.sentence: I feel you—the extra client requests have made this week ridiculously busy.
uses.tip: Follow it with a specific observation so it does not sound like empty reassurance.

uses.where: Catching up with a friend · someone cancels a plan
uses.sentence: I feel you; after the trip you had, I would have wanted to cancel something too.
uses.tip: It sounds conversational and caring, especially among people who already know each other.

uses.sentence: I feel you, especially if you had to deal with the train cancellation on your own.
uses.tip: Keep it brief in a message, then add a question or a helpful suggestion if you want to continue the conversation.

origin.summary: The wording is literal, but its conversational use as a sign of empathy developed from broader everyday expressions of shared feelings.

timeline.text: The literal sense means sharing another person’s feelings.
The expression becomes established in casual English as a way to show understanding.
It is common in everyday speech, online messages and supportive responses.

similar: I know exactly what you mean
cards.pitfall: It can sound vague or slightly dismissive if you do not make clear what you understand about the other person’s experience.

cards.hint: a desire that may not be possible
cards.meaning: Used to express a hope, regret or wish for something that is not possible or is unlikely to happen.
cards.nuance: It can sound sincere, nostalgic or frustrated depending on the context. In a work setting, it may seem passive, so pair it with a clear request when you need action.

uses.sentence: I wish we had more time to review the figures before the meeting.
uses.tip: After expressing regret, state what you need in a direct, polite way.

uses.sentence: I wish you’d told me earlier, but I completely understand why you couldn’t.
uses.tip: Use it to begin gently when raising a disappointment with someone.

uses.sentence: I wish we could move the deadline, but the delivery date has to stay.
uses.tip: Keep it honest but soft; follow it with the reason and next step.

origin.summary: The phrase grew from the English verb wish, which has long been used for hoping for or asking for something.

timeline.text: The ancestor of wish was used for hoping, praying or wanting something to happen.
Wish became common in statements expressing hope, desire and regret.
The phrase “I wish” remains a natural everyday way to talk about unreal or unlikely possibilities.

cards.pitfall: In professional messages, “I wish” can sound passive or indirect, so add a specific request or explanation.

cards.meaning: Remaining faithful to someone through both difficult times and happy times.
cards.nuance: It expresses lasting loyalty, especially in marriage, and can also be used more broadly for committed relationships. The traditional wording sounds ceremonial and personal.
cards.literal: The person stays with their partner whether they are ill or healthy.

uses.sentence: We’re all in this together, in sickness and in health, and we’ll keep sharing the workload.
uses.tip: Use it to signal dependable teamwork, not to dismiss someone’s illness.

uses.sentence: Here’s to a marriage that stands in sickness and in health, with patience, trust and plenty of laughter.
uses.tip: This is especially familiar in wedding vows and toasts.

uses.sentence: Wishing you a life together in sickness and in health, filled with love, understanding and joyful memories.
uses.tip: It suits a heartfelt message but can sound formal or traditional.

origin.summary: The phrase comes from the traditional Christian marriage vow promising love and faithfulness during illness and health. Its exact wording developed through different versions of the Book of Common Prayer and other religious texts.

timeline.text: The Book of Common Prayer uses the vow “in sickness and in health” in its marriage service.
Related wording appeared in medieval English marriage vows, though earlier versions were not identical.
The phrase remains part of many wedding vows and is also used figuratively to express lasting loyalty.

cards.pitfall: Because it comes from marriage vows, using it about friends or colleagues may sound overly dramatic unless the relationship is genuinely close.

cards.meaning: Something that is not important or worth worrying about.
cards.nuance: It reassures someone that a minor issue does not matter. It is informal and may sound dismissive if the other person is genuinely upset.
cards.literal: The matter is not a serious problem.

uses.where: Colleague apologising for a small delay
uses.sentence: The report was ten minutes late, but it’s no big deal.
uses.tip: Use it to reassure a colleague about a minor inconvenience.

uses.sentence: If you can’t make it, that’s no big deal—we can reschedule.
uses.tip: It sounds friendly when the inconvenience is genuinely small.

uses.where: Casual message about a minor change
uses.sentence: I’ve moved our coffee to three o’clock; it’s no big deal if that no longer works.
uses.tip: It suits informal messages, but avoid it when the issue needs attention.

origin.summary: The expression developed from everyday talk about whether something was a serious matter. Its current meaning is informal and well established.

timeline.text: People used variations of “big deal” to ask whether something mattered.
“No big deal” became a common informal way to dismiss a minor matter.
It is widely used in casual American and British English.

cards.pitfall: Avoid saying “no big deal” when the other person is distressed or the problem clearly needs attention.

cards.register: Common at work and in casual conversation
cards.meaning: A reassurance that you are not angry or personally offended by something someone has said or done.
cards.nuance: It is usually friendly and conciliatory, often used after disagreement, criticism or a failed negotiation. It may sound slightly formal in some casual settings, where “all good” or “no worries” can feel more natural.
cards.literal: Someone has hurt another person’s feelings, but the person says there is no lasting anger or resentment.

uses.sentence: I’m sorry the feedback was direct, but no hard feelings—we both want this launch to succeed.
uses.tip: Use it to ease tension after criticism or disagreement.

uses.sentence: I know you were looking forward to dinner, but no hard feelings—we can reschedule for next week.
uses.tip: It reassures someone that you are not upset while leaving the door open.

uses.sentence: We approached the proposal differently, but there are no hard feelings between us.
uses.tip: It can soften a message, but consider naming the disagreement more directly.

origin.summary: The phrase developed from the older expression “hard feelings,” meaning anger or resentment. Its exact first recorded use is uncertain, but it was established long before it became common in modern conversation.

timeline.text: The expression “hard feelings” referred to anger, dislike or lasting resentment between people.
“No hard feelings” appeared as a way of denying or dismissing lasting resentment.
It is a familiar reassurance after arguments, criticism and broken plans.

cards.pitfall: Saying “no hard feelings” does not automatically repair a relationship; acknowledge the other person’s perspective if the disagreement mattered.

cards.meaning: Not enthusiastic, interested or convinced about something at the moment.
cards.nuance: Often used to describe a lack of motivation or emotional connection. It can sound honest and relaxed, but too much use may suggest disengagement rather than a thoughtful objection.

uses.sentence: Honestly, I’m just not feeling it today, so could we postpone the presentation until tomorrow?
uses.tip: Pair it with a practical alternative so it doesn’t sound like a refusal to help.

uses.sentence: I’m not feeling it tonight, but send me the photos if you all go out.
uses.tip: Use it when your energy is low rather than when you strongly dislike the plan.

uses.where: Message to a friend · declining an invite
uses.sentence: Thanks for inviting me, but I’m not feeling it, so I’ll sit this one out.
uses.tip: It works in casual messages; give a clearer reason in formal communication.

origin.summary: Likely developed from the ordinary phrase “not feel it,” meaning not experiencing an emotion, sensation or strong inclination. Its modern use became especially common in informal speech.

timeline.text: The literal idea is not experiencing a feeling or sensation.
Casual usage expands to mean lacking enthusiasm, interest or conviction.
Common in relaxed conversations about mood, motivation and social plans.

cards.pitfall: It can sound vague. If you need someone to understand a decision clearly, explain what you do not feel enthusiastic about.

cards.meaning: Speaking only a little, often because you are quiet, reserved or have little to contribute.
cards.nuance: This can sound neutral and descriptive, but it may imply that someone is unusually quiet or has little to say. In a work context, it can sometimes suggest that a person is holding back an opinion.

uses.sentence: Maya was not saying much, so I asked whether she had concerns about the new schedule.
uses.tip: Use it to describe someone’s level of participation, but ask directly if you need their view.

uses.sentence: He was not saying much at first, but he opened up once the topic turned to music.
uses.tip: This is a gentle way to note that someone is quiet without making it sound like criticism.

uses.sentence: The client was not saying much during the call, although she clearly wanted time to review the proposal.
uses.tip: Use it when the amount of speech matters, not when you want to record someone’s exact words.

origin.summary: This is an ordinary English phrase made from a negative form of “say much,” rather than a fixed idiom with a clear origin.

timeline.text: The expression developed from the plain-language idea that a person “says little” or “does not say much.”
Similar constructions using “not saying much” appear in ordinary written and spoken English.
It remains a common everyday expression for describing quiet or limited participation.

cards.pitfall: It can sound like a judgment, so pair it with context when describing someone who is simply thinking or taking time to respond.

cards.meaning: A reassuring way to tell someone that there is no need to feel concerned.
cards.nuance: Warm and casual, it is often used when someone mentions a problem or worry. It can also sound a little dismissive if you do not acknowledge the concern first.

uses.sentence: The report will arrive a little late, but there’s not to worry; the deadline is still Friday.
uses.tip: Use it when you can reassure the person with clear information.

uses.sentence: You’ll still get there before the party starts, so not to worry.
uses.tip: This sounds friendly and informal, especially with people you know well.

uses.sentence: There’s not to worry about the invoice; I’ll check the payment and let you know today.
uses.tip: Pair it with a concrete next step so it does not sound dismissive.

origin.summary: This phrase likely developed from the older expression “no need to worry,” with “not” replacing “no need” in everyday speech.

timeline.text: The expression “no need to worry” was used to offer reassurance.
Shortened forms such as “not to worry” became common in informal English.
It remains a casual way to reassure someone in conversation and writing.

cards.pitfall: Avoid saying “not to worry” when the situation is serious or the other person wants empathy rather than reassurance.

cards.register: Common in formal writing and conversation
cards.meaning: Very close to reaching a serious or important point, especially a crisis or major change.
cards.nuance: It adds drama and signals that action is urgent. It is often followed by “of” and a noun, such as “on the brink of collapse.”
cards.literal: Balanced at the edge of something, such as a cliff, with a steep drop below.

uses.sentence: Our payment system is on the brink of failing, so we need technical support now.
uses.tip: Use it to stress urgency, then follow with the action needed.

uses.sentence: We were on the brink of arguing, but she apologised before the conversation got worse.
uses.tip: This version can describe the moment just before conflict or another event.

uses.sentence: The small business is on the brink of closure after months of falling sales.
uses.tip: It works well in reporting because it clearly signals an imminent outcome.

origin.summary: The expression probably grew from the literal image of someone standing at the edge of a cliff or precipice. Its figurative use for being close to a crisis developed from that danger and suspense.

timeline.text: The literal expression referred to being positioned at the edge of a steep drop.
Writers began using the image to describe situations involving extreme danger or uncertainty.
It commonly means that something serious is about to happen, especially a crisis or collapse.

cards.pitfall: Usually use “on the brink of” before a noun or gerund: “on the brink of shutting down,” not “on the brink to shut down.”

cards.register: Common at work and in conversation
cards.meaning: To express one’s deepest feelings fully and without holding back.
cards.nuance: It suggests an intense, sincere emotional release, often involving speech, music or creativity. It can sound heartfelt, though it may feel dramatic in ordinary situations.
cards.literal: Taking one’s heart out and exposing it, as if revealing every feeling inside.

uses.where: Team discussion · sharing a difficult experience
uses.sentence: During the review, she poured her heart out about the problems she had faced.
uses.tip: It suits a sincere personal account rather than a brief status update.

uses.where: Catching up · hearing a friend’s news
uses.sentence: He poured his heart out about how much he had missed his family.
uses.tip: Use it when the speaker is being unusually open or emotional.

uses.sentence: I poured my heart out in the letter because I wanted her to know how grateful I was.
uses.tip: It adds warmth and emotional weight, so avoid it in routine messages.

origin.summary: The image probably comes from expressions such as “cry your heart out” and “scream your heart out,” in which a person’s deepest emotions are imagined as coming directly from the heart.

timeline.text: Similar wording appeared in expressions about crying or speaking from the heart.
Forms such as “pour your heart out” became common for intense emotional expression.
People use it for heartfelt conversations, creative work and emotional performances.

similar: from the bottom of your heart
cards.pitfall: “One’s heart out” normally appears in a fuller phrase such as “pour one’s heart out” or “with all one’s heart out,” rather than standing alone.

cards.meaning: To present your abilities, value or prospects as lower than they really are.
cards.nuance: It describes being too modest, self-doubting or unwilling to claim what you bring. It often appears when discussing pay, promotion, qualifications or an application.
cards.literal: To sell your worth for less than it is actually worth.

uses.where: Salary discussion · asking for a raise
uses.sentence: Don’t sell yourself short by accepting less than the role and your experience require.
uses.tip: Use it to encourage someone to state their value clearly and confidently.

uses.sentence: You’re skilled enough for that role, so try not to sell yourself short when you introduce yourself.
uses.tip: It works well as warm encouragement, but avoid making someone feel defensive.

uses.where: Cover email · applying for a job
uses.sentence: Describe the scope of your work without selling yourself short or apologising for your experience.
uses.tip: In this form, the highlight must match the exact wording used in the sentence.

origin.summary: Likely developed from older trade-related language about selling goods below their value, then extended to people understating their abilities or prospects.

timeline.text: The expression “sell short” referred to selling something for less than its usual or fair value.
People began using the idea of selling below value figuratively when speaking about personal chances or worth.
“Sell oneself short” is common advice about presenting your abilities and negotiating your value.

cards.pitfall: Some modesty can sound polite, but this phrase points to a real risk of being paid less, overlooked or hired for the wrong role.
